t: Maximum Alternating Subarray Sum - Two-Slot Kadane
o: Each subarray is scored by restarting the +/- alternation at its own first element: nums[i] - nums[i+1] + nums[i+2] - .... In example 1, the window [3,-1,1] scores 3 - (-1) + 1 = 5, the best anywhere. The subarray must be non-empty, so when every element is negative the answer is the largest single element rather than 0. With n up to 10^5, evaluating all O(n^2) subwindows individually is off the table and a Kadane-style linear pass is needed.
k: Signs depend only on position parity relative to the subarray start, so there are exactly two alignments of interest.
Negating odd-indexed elements and running standard Kadane covers windows that start on even indices; negating even-indexed ones covers the rest.
A single DP pass tracking "best alternating sum ending here in a + slot" and "in a - slot" merges both alignments.

a.i: Fix each start index, accumulate the running alternating sum while extending the end, and record every intermediate value, since every prefix of the window is itself a scored subarray. A direct translation of the scoring definition; quadratic.
s: Loop over start i with accumulator s = 0.
Extend j from i onward, adding nums[j] when (j - i) is even and subtracting otherwise.
Update the answer with s after each extension.
a.t: O(n^2) - every subwindow prefix is evaluated once, ~10^10 steps at n = 10^5.

a.i: Flip the sign of every odd-indexed element; then any window's ordinary sum equals the alternating sum of the corresponding window starting at an even index. Flipping even indices instead handles windows that start odd. Two textbook Kadane runs over non-empty windows and take the larger result.
s: Build f1 by negating odd positions and f2 by negating even positions.
Run Kadane (cur = max(x, cur + x), never emptying the window) on each sequence.
Return the maximum of the two results.
a.sp: O(n) - the flipped copies (avoidable by flipping on the fly).

a.i: Maintain pos = best alternating sum of a subarray ending at the current index whose current element carries a + sign, and neg likewise for a - sign. A + slot either starts fresh (x) or extends a preceding - slot (neg + x); a - slot must follow a + slot (pos_prev - x) because a subarray can never open with subtraction. Initializing both slots to -infinity enforces that rule, and the answer is the best value ever seen in either slot.
s: For each x, update pos = max(x, neg + x) and neg = old_pos - x simultaneously.
Fold both slots into ans after each element.
a.t: O(n) - one pass with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) - two scalars regardless of input size.

w: The classic mistake is letting global index parity decide the signs - alignment is relative to the subarray start, which is why two alignments (or the paired-slot DP) are required. Another trap is returning 0 on all-negative inputs; the window must be non-empty, so [3,-1,1,2]-style reasoning on [-3,-1] yields -1. Present the flip-plus-Kadane idea if clarity matters most and the paired DP as the polished O(1)-space finish. Follow-ups: return the actual subarray (remember where each slot run started), or maximize over subsequences instead of subarrays.
